title: Municipal EV Charging Infrastructure Planning Guide 2026
summary: A planning guide for municipal EV charging infrastructure: needs assessment, site selection, funding, procurement, and operations for city charging.
body_markdown:
Public EV charging has become core municipal infrastructure. Residents treat it the way they treat streetlights and parking meters: a service the city provides, maintains, and answers for.


That expectation is where municipal charging programs run into trouble. The planning phase usually goes well. Cities run good community engagement, select reasonable sites, and win grant funding. The difficulty arrives eighteen months after the ribbon-cutting, when a third of the ports are offline, the vendor agreement contains no enforceable performance standard, and a council member is asking why the city spent $400,000 on chargers that do not work.


This guide covers the full arc of a municipal charging program: assessing need, selecting sites, assembling funding, running a procurement that protects public investment, managing installation, and operating a network that performs over a ten-year horizon. We wrote it for city planners, municipal energy managers, public works directors, sustainability coordinators, transportation planners, and the fleet managers who increasingly share this infrastructure.


Planning a network for your community?[Request a demo](https://www.ampup.io/request-a-demo) to see how AmpUp supports[municipal charging programs](https://www.ampup.io/use-cases/ev-charging-management-for-municipalities) .


‍


**TL;DR How do municipalities plan and implement EV charging infrastructure?**


Municipal EV charging infrastructure planning follows a five-phase framework that balances community need, financial sustainability, and long-term operational performance:


- **Phase 1: Needs assessment and goal setting (2 to 4 months).** Analyze current EV registrations by ZIP code, project five to ten year growth against state policy, identify neighborhoods without home charging access, establish quantifiable targets such as "300 public charging ports by 2029," and align the program with adopted climate action commitments.
- **Phase 2: Site selection and prioritization (3 to 6 months).** Evaluate candidate locations against electrical capacity, parking dwell time, destination proximity, community need, and property control, while running public engagement that gathers real input on preferred locations.
- **Phase 3: Funding and financial planning (4 to 8 months).** Develop capital and operating budgets, pursue state energy office and utility programs, evaluate federal corridor funding where applicable, and structure public-private partnerships that reduce municipal capital exposure without surrendering policy control.
- **Phase 4: Procurement and installation (6 to 12 months).** Issue RFPs requiring OCPP compliance and enforceable uptime and session success standards, select a hardware-agnostic charging management platform that supports multiple manufacturers, and coordinate electrical work with your utility.
- **Phase 5: Operations and continuous improvement (ongoing).** Implement monitoring and maintenance that sustains a 98.5% charging session success rate, track utilization and adjust pricing and access policy, publish performance data, and expand based on demonstrated demand.


## Why Municipal EV Charging Infrastructure Is Essential


### The Role of Local Government in Transportation Electrification


Home and workplace charging cover most daily driving for most EV owners. Local government's role is the space those two leave behind, and that space is concentrated in identifiable places and populations.


Renters and[multifamily residents](https://www.ampup.io/blog/multifamily-ev-charging-solutions-guide) are the clearest case. A household without a dedicated parking space and a 240V circuit cannot treat home charging as a default, which makes public charging the deciding factor in whether an EV is viable at all. Cities that want EV adoption to extend past single-family homeowners have to build for that population deliberately, because the market will not do it on its own. Charging operators site for utilization, and utilization follows existing EV density, which produces a loop that leaves lower-income and higher-density neighborhoods last in line.


Local government also fills the gap between short-range daily driving and longer regional travel. Corridor charging gets federal attention, but the more common municipal gap is the intermediate trip: the resident who drives 60 miles to a regional hospital, the visitor staying two nights downtown, the commuter parking at a transit center all day.


Finally, cities carry a leadership role that goes beyond their own asset base. Municipal decisions on permitting timelines, building code requirements for EV-ready parking, and curbside charging policy shape what private developers build. A city that streamlines EV charger permitting to a ten-day over-the-counter process will see more private charging installed than one that routes every application through a three-month discretionary review, regardless of how many public ports it funds directly.


### Federal and State Mandates Driving Municipal Action


The policy landscape has changed substantially since 2024, and planning documents written before 2025 will misinform your team. Here is where things actually stand.


The[NEVI Formula Program](https://afdc.energy.gov/laws/12744) . Funded at $5 billion through FY 2026, the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program was paused in February 2025 pending federal review. Following litigation and a court order requiring release of the withheld funds,[FHWA issued revised interim guidance in August 2025](https://afdc.energy.gov/laws/12744) that replaced all prior NEVI guidance and allowed states to resubmit deployment plans. States have been reopening solicitations since.


The revised guidance changed the program in ways that benefit cities specifically. The strict 50-mile corridor spacing requirement was removed in favor of state discretion, and states that certify their Alternative Fuel Corridors as fully built out can direct remaining NEVI funds to off-corridor locations, including community charging sites and municipal facilities. Federal cost share remains up to 80%. States may also apply NEVI funds to medium- and heavy-duty charging, which matters for transit and public works fleets.


**The 30C tax credit has expired.** The Alternative Fuel Vehicle Refueling Property Credit expired June 30, 2026, and direct pay eligibility for tax-exempt entities lapsed earlier. Any financial model still carrying 30C needs revision.


**Federal equity requirements have moved to states.** The Justice40 Initiative and the federal Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool were rescinded in January 2025. Equity obligations have not disappeared, but their source has changed. We cover the practical implications in detail below.


**State policy is now doing more of the work.** Zero-emission vehicle sales requirements, state energy office grant programs, and utility make-ready programs are the more reliable planning anchors in most jurisdictions. Several states have also adopted their own EV-ready building code provisions and charging deployment targets that apply to municipal facilities directly. Check your state energy office and your public utilities commission before you check federal sources, because in 2026 that is where the binding requirements and the available money are more likely to be.


**Fleet requirements.** Many states maintain zero-emission procurement requirements for state and local government fleets, often with phased compliance dates. Where those apply, fleet charging infrastructure is not discretionary, which changes the internal funding conversation considerably. Our[guide to EV charging funding for fleets](https://www.ampup.io/blog/the-fleet-operators-guide-to-ev-charging-funding) covers the programs that apply.


### Benefits Beyond Climate: Economic Development and Equity


Climate goals bring most municipal charging programs to the council agenda. They are rarely what gets the program funded. Build the case on the other benefits as well.


**Destination spending.** EV drivers charging downtown are parked for two to four hours, and they spend that time somewhere. Charging availability influences where regional visitors choose to stop, which is why business improvement districts are often the most enthusiastic partners in a municipal charging conversation.


**Site selection and business attraction.** Charging availability now appears in corporate site selection criteria, particularly for employers with fleet operations or sustainability commitments. It is a modest factor, but it is a real one, and it costs a city nothing to be able to answer the question well.


**Local employment.** Installation and ongoing maintenance are local trades work. Electrical contracting, site preparation, and service calls are not outsourced to a distant headquarters. Cities that include local hiring provisions in charging contracts can make this explicit.


**Transportation access.** For a household weighing an EV purchase, reliable public charging within a reasonable distance is the difference between a viable option and an impractical one. Municipal charging expands who gets to participate in lower per-mile transportation costs.


**Air quality.** Emissions reductions from transportation electrification are concentrated along high-traffic corridors, which in most cities overlap with the neighborhoods that have historically borne the worst air quality burden. This is a public health argument as much as a climate one, and it tends to land differently with a council.


## Phase 1: Conducting a Comprehensive Needs Assessment


### Analyzing Current EV Adoption and Future Projections


Start with state DMV registration data at the ZIP code level. It is the most defensible baseline available, and it routinely contradicts staff intuition about where EV owners actually live.


From there, project forward. Adoption tends to follow an S-curve rather than a straight line, which means a community early in its adoption cycle will underestimate demand badly if it extrapolates linearly from the last three years. Build a range rather than a single number, and document your assumptions so the projection can be revisited without redoing the whole analysis.


Inputs worth incorporating:


- Historical registration growth in your jurisdiction and in comparable jurisdictions that are further along
- State policy effects, including any zero-emission sales requirements and their compliance timeline
- Vehicle availability and price trends, including the used EV market, which drives adoption in lower-income households more than new sales do
- Changes to purchase incentives, which shifted significantly in 2025 and 2026 and affect near-term adoption rates


The[Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center](https://afdc.energy.gov/) maintains registration data and modeling tools, including EVI-Pro Lite, which estimates charging infrastructure requirements for a defined geography and vehicle population. Run it before your own numbers reach a council packet.


A common planning assumption is designing for several times the current EV population over a five to seven year horizon. The multiplier varies widely by state policy and local income profile, so treat it as a starting point for discussion rather than a figure to put in a staff report.


### Understanding Your Community's Charging Gap


Demand projection tells you how much. Gap analysis tells you where, and it is the more useful of the two for site selection decisions.


**Home charging access by housing type.** Pull housing stock data and identify the share of households without dedicated off-street parking. This is your core public charging constituency, and it is usually geographically concentrated.


**Workplace charging availability.** Survey major employers. Where workplace charging is common, public daytime demand is lower and your emphasis should shift toward evening and weekend locations. A short survey through your economic development office or chamber of commerce is usually enough.


**Public charging inventory.** Map what exists, including privately owned sites the public can use. Note reliability as well as count, since an unreliable station is not meaningfully serving anyone. Driver-reported data from charging apps is useful here.


**Regional and corridor needs.** Coordinate with your metropolitan planning organization (MPO), and start with its regional EV plan and travel data if it has them. Corridor gaps are often better addressed regionally than by any single jurisdiction.


**Visitor demand.** For cities with meaningful tourism or event traffic, visitor charging is a distinct demand profile with different timing and different location logic than resident charging.


### Stakeholder Engagement and Public Input


Engagement is both a planning input and a political requirement. Done well, it produces better site selection and a constituency that defends the program when it hits difficulty. Done as a formality, it produces a record of consultation and little else.


Approaches that work:


- **Community workshops in the neighborhoods under consideration** , not only at city hall. Attendance at a downtown evening meeting skews heavily toward people who already own EVs.
- **Online surveys and mapping tools** that let residents mark preferred locations. These scale well and reach people who cannot attend meetings, though they underrepresent residents with limited internet access.
- **Focus groups with distinct populations** : current EV owners, prospective buyers, and residents in neighborhoods with low home charging access. Their concerns differ substantially.
- **Business community outreach** through chambers of commerce, downtown associations, and business improvement districts. These groups often become funding partners.
- **Regional coordination** with neighboring jurisdictions, which prevents duplicated effort and strengthens joint grant applications.


The National League of Cities[primer for municipal officials](https://www.nlc.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/EV-Charging-Brief.pdf) is a useful framing document to share with council members new to the topic.


Be specific about what is actually open for input. Residents can tell the difference between genuine consultation on site selection and a presentation of decisions already made, and the second erodes trust you will need later.


### Setting Clear, Measurable Goals


Vague goals produce vague accountability. Set targets a council can measure and staff can report against:


- **Port count by year** , split between Level 2 and DC fast
- **Geographic distribution** , expressed as ports per capita, ports per square mile, or the share of residents within a defined drive time
- **Distribution across neighborhoods** , particularly those with the lowest home charging access
- **Utilization targets** , measured as sessions per port per day, with a realistic ramp period built in
- **Reliability targets** , stated separately as uptime and session success rate
- **Cost recovery expectations** , stated honestly, including which sites are expected to operate at a subsidy and why
- **Alignment with climate action plan milestones** , so the charging program reports into an existing framework rather than creating a parallel one


Set the reliability targets now rather than at procurement. They become RFP requirements in Phase 4, and a target established through public process is far harder for a vendor to negotiate away.


## Phase 2: Strategic Site Selection and Prioritization


### Evaluation Criteria for Charging Locations


Score candidate sites against a consistent rubric rather than settling them one at a time. A documented scoring framework also gives you a defensible answer when a council member asks why their district was not first.


- **Electrical capacity:** existing service, available headroom, distance to adequate service, and estimated upgrade cost
- **Parking availability:** actual dwell time, turnover rate, and current utilization, since a lot that is full at noon may be empty at 7 PM
- **Proximity to destinations:** retail, dining, recreation, civic buildings, and transit
- **Visibility and accessibility:** ADA-compliant spaces and pathways, legible wayfinding, and lighting that makes the site usable and safe after dark
- **Property ownership:** municipal property is the fastest path; private partnerships expand reach but add time
- **Community need:** neighborhoods with the lowest home charging access and the highest share of renters


Weight these explicitly. Most cities find that electrical capacity and property control dominate the practical outcome, which is worth knowing before you promise a specific neighborhood a specific timeline.


### Location Types and Use Case Matching


Dwell time determines charging level more reliably than any other factor. Match them deliberately:


Location type Typical dwell Recommended level Notes


Downtown commercial districts 2 to 4 hours Level 2


Pair with existing parking time limits

Weekend-peaked demand


Municipal buildings and libraries 1 to 8 hours Level 2


, mixed access Staff by day, public by evening


Transit centers and park-and-rides 8+ hours Level 2


, limited DC fast Long dwell favors Level 2 economics


Highway corridors 20 to 45 minutes DC fast


NEVI-relevant site selection


Residential neighborhood hubs Overnight Level 2


Serves households without home charging


Cost category Typical range


Level 2 port, installed $3,000 to $7,000


DC fast port, installed $75,000 to $150,000


Electrical service upgrade, per site $20,000 to $150,000

KPI Target

The most common and most expensive site selection error is specifying DC fast charging where dwell time is long. It multiplies capital cost, triggers demand charges, and delivers no benefit to a driver parked at a library for three hours. The reverse error, Level 2 on a highway corridor, is less common but equally unhelpful.


One note on transit centers: the intuition that commuters need fast charging is usually wrong. A vehicle parked from 7 AM to 6 PM is the ideal Level 2 candidate, and the capital savings let you serve four to six times as many vehicles for the same budget.


### Equity-Focused Site Selection Framework


The federal framework that governed this work through 2024 no longer exists, so the practical approach has changed.


**What changed.** The Justice40 Initiative, which directed 40% of the benefits of covered federal programs to disadvantaged communities, was rescinded in January 2025 along with the Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool that defined those communities. Federal grant applications no longer carry Justice40 documentation requirements.


**What still applies.** State and local requirements are now the operative framework, and in many states they are substantial. California's[CalEnviroScreen](https://oehha.ca.gov/calenviroscreen/report/calenviroscreen-40) remains in active use and is referenced in state program eligibility. Other states maintain their own screening tools and equity criteria in energy office grant programs. Local equity indices adopted by council remain fully enforceable as municipal policy regardless of federal changes.


**Practical approach for 2026.** Build your distribution framework on criteria you control and can defend:


- Home charging access by census tract, derived from housing type and parking availability data you already hold
- Renter share and multifamily density
- Your state's screening tool where one exists
- Any equity criteria already adopted in your climate action plan or general plan


The advantage of local criteria is durability. A distribution framework grounded in your own housing data and adopted by your own council does not change when federal executive orders do, which is worth something given the last two years.


**Beyond site selection.** Location alone does not produce access. Community benefit agreements, local hiring provisions, multilingual signage and app support, and non-app payment options all determine whether a station in a given neighborhood is genuinely usable by the people who live there.


### Electrical Infrastructure and Utility Coordination


Start the utility conversation in Phase 2, not Phase 4. Service upgrade timelines are the single most common source of municipal project delay.


**Capacity analysis.** Ask your utility for distribution system capacity information at each candidate site. Many utilities maintain hosting capacity maps that will save you weeks. Where they do not, an early conversation with a utility planning engineer will still narrow your list quickly.


**Make-ready programs.** Where they exist, utility make-ready programs cover electrical infrastructure from the transformer to the charger stub-out, frequently the largest single offset available to a municipal project. Eligibility windows and program budgets close, so confirm current status rather than relying on last year's information.


**Service upgrade costs.** Budget $20,000 to $150,000 per site depending on distance to adequate service. That range is wide enough to reorder your priority list entirely, which is precisely why the analysis belongs in site selection.


**Timeline.** Plan 6 to 18 months for major electrical work. Simple service additions land at the short end. New transformer installations land at the long end, and occasionally beyond it.


**Three-phase power.** DC fast charging requires it. Confirm availability before committing to a DC fast site, because extending three-phase service can dominate a project budget.


[Load management](https://www.ampup.io/blog/ev-advanced-load-management) **.** Where capacity is constrained, load management software lets you deploy more ports on existing service by distributing available power across active sessions. This is often the difference between a site that works within current capacity and a site that requires a service upgrade.


### Property Partnerships and Easement Agreements


**Municipal property first.** City hall, libraries, community centers, parks, and municipal lots are the fastest path. You control the property, the approval process is internal, and you avoid negotiating access terms with a third party.


**Private property partnerships** expand reach into retail corridors and multifamily properties where the need is often greatest. Expect longer timelines and more complex agreements.


Terms to settle before installation:


- **Lease versus easement structure** , and which fits your municipal code and the property owner's financing
- **Revenue sharing** , if any, and how it is calculated and reported
- **Term length** , typically 10 to 20 years to amortize the investment. Shorter terms rarely justify the capital
- **Maintenance and liability allocation** , specifically who is responsible for the equipment, the parking surface, snow removal, and signage
- **Insurance and indemnification** requirements consistent with your risk management policy
- **What happens at termination** , including equipment ownership and site restoration


Involve your city attorney early. Easement and revenue-sharing structures are unfamiliar territory for many municipal legal departments, and discovering that in month eight is expensive.


## Phase 3: Funding Strategies and Financial Planning


### Federal Grant Programs and Application Strategy


Federal funding in 2026 requires more attention to current status than it did two years ago.


**NEVI Formula Program.** Active following the 2025 reset described above. Administered through state energy offices and DOTs, with up to 80% federal cost share. Timeline from application to deployment has historically run 18 to 24 months. The August 2025 guidance expanded eligibility beyond corridors for states that certify their corridors as fully built out, which opens community charging locations in those states. Availability and round timing vary significantly by state, so start with your state agency rather than federal guidance.


**Federal formula funds programmed through your MPO.** CMAQ, available in air quality nonattainment and maintenance areas, lists EV charging as an eligible use. STBG funds can also support charging, and in larger metro areas the MPO selects projects for its share. The Carbon Reduction Program has funded charging as well, but its future is uncertain in the current reauthorization debate, so confirm availability before building a plan around it. All of these generally require the project to be in your MPO’s Transportation Improvement Program. They are less visible than headline federal programs and frequently overlooked.


**EPA programs.** Clean Ports and the[Clean School Bus Program](https://www.epa.gov/cleanschoolbus) remain relevant for cities with port operations or school district partnerships. Confirm current funding status and application cycles directly with EPA, since several programs have been restructured.


**Community Project Funding.** Congressionally directed spending remains available through your federal delegation. Charging infrastructure is an eligible category. Requests are submitted through House and Senate offices on an annual cycle with early-year deadlines.


**Application strategy.** Federal applications reward specificity. Have your site list, electrical assessments, cost estimates, and utility correspondence assembled before the notice of funding opportunity opens. Cities that start assembling documentation when the NOFO drops are usually too late.


### State and Local Funding Sources


State and local sources have become the more dependable backbone of municipal charging finance.


- **State energy office grant programs.** The most consistently available source. Program structure varies widely, and many run multiple rounds per year.
- **California-specific programs.** CALeVIP, California Energy Commission grants, and Low Carbon Fuel Standard credit revenue remain significant for California jurisdictions. LCFS credits in particular generate ongoing revenue from charging operations rather than one-time capital.
- **Regional air quality management district funding.** Often available in nonattainment regions, with lighter application requirements than state or federal programs.
- **Transportation development impact fees.** Where your fee schedule permits, charging infrastructure can be an eligible use.
- **Municipal and green bonds.** Appropriate for larger multi-site deployments with a defined revenue model. Green bond designation can improve pricing and broaden the investor pool.
- **Cap-and-trade or carbon revenue.** Where your state allocates such revenue to transportation electrification, local governments are frequently eligible recipients.


AmpUp maintains a current list of[EV incentives and rebates](https://www.ampup.io/resources/ev-charger-rebates-and-incentives) by jurisdiction.


### Utility Programs and Incentives


Utility programs deserve separate attention because they are frequently the largest single offset and the most commonly missed.


- **Make-ready programs.** The utility funds electrical infrastructure up to the charger, sometimes including the charger itself. Coverage varies from partial to complete.
- **Equipment and installation rebates.** Per-port rebates, sometimes at higher levels for sites serving multifamily or lower-income areas.
- **EV-specific rate schedules.** Many utilities offer commercial EV rates that reduce or eliminate demand charges during a ramp period. This can be worth more over ten years than the installation rebate.
- **Demand response and managed charging incentives.** Ongoing payments for allowing the utility to modulate charging during grid peaks. Requires a platform that can respond to utility signals.
- **On-bill financing.** Some utilities finance infrastructure costs through the electricity bill, which avoids a capital appropriation entirely.
- **Co-investment partnerships.** Some utilities will co-invest in municipal charging directly, particularly at sites that support their own load management objectives.


Ask your utility account representative about all six categories explicitly. These programs are not always well publicized, and eligibility is frequently broader than the marketing suggests.


### Public-Private Partnership Models


Three structures cover most municipal deployments, each with a different trade-off between capital exposure and control.


**Full private investment.** A charging operator funds, installs, owns, and operates under a franchise or site license agreement. The city contributes site access and permitting support. Minimal municipal capital, and correspondingly minimal municipal control over pricing, access policy, and site selection priorities. Best suited to high-utilization commercial locations where the operator's economics work without subsidy.


**Joint investment.** The city funds infrastructure, typically the electrical work, and the private partner funds and operates the charging equipment. Revenue sharing in the 60/40 to 70/30 range is common, with the split favoring whichever party carries more capital. This model works well when your make-ready costs are covered by a utility program, since the city's actual contribution becomes modest.


**Municipal ownership with managed services.** The city owns the assets and contracts operations, monitoring, and maintenance. This preserves full control over pricing, access policy, and expansion sequencing while transferring operational risk and staffing burden. It is the model most often chosen by cities with equity commitments, because it is the only one in which the city sets pricing at sites where the economics do not stand alone.


Whichever structure you select, write performance requirements into the agreement. Specify uptime and session success standards, reporting cadence, response times, and a remedy for sustained non-performance. A partnership without an enforceable performance standard is not a partnership.


Also specify term length, renewal conditions, technology refresh obligations, and how risk is allocated for equipment failure, underutilization, and obsolescence.


### Developing Sustainable Operating Models


Realistic figures for budgeting:


Cost category Typical range


Level 2 port, installed $3,000 to $7,000


DC fast port, installed $75,000 to $150,000


Electrical service upgrade, per site $20,000 to $150,000


ADA compliance work, per site Varies by existing site conditions


Break-even timeline 3 to 7 years, utilization dependent


Operating expenses that belong in the model: electricity including demand charges, preventive and reactive maintenance, network software, payment processing fees, customer support, and periodic equipment replacement across a seven to ten year lifecycle.


Additional ADA compliance expenses may be required depending on the condition of the site. Accessible space dimensions, curb ramps, path-of-travel regrading, and signage are frequently not budgeted at the concept stage, and they are least predictable at older municipal lots that predate current accessibility standards. Get an accessibility assessment into your cost estimate before the number reaches a council packet.


On the revenue side, model conservatively. Utilization ramps slowly, and first-year projections built on mature-network assumptions are the most common source of a difficult second-year budget conversation. The[AmpUp revenue calculator](https://www.ampup.io/resources/ev-charging-revenue-calculator) lets you test assumptions against your own utility rates before they reach a budget document.


Model the subsidy explicitly for sites built primarily for access rather than revenue. Cities get into political trouble when they present an access-driven site using the same financial expectations as a downtown site, then have to explain the shortfall two years later. Naming it upfront as a public service decision, with a specific annual cost, is a far better position.


The[managed services option](https://www.ampup.io/products/managed-ev-charging) converts variable operational costs into a predictable monthly figure, which is easier to budget and to defend than a line item that fluctuates with equipment failures.


## Phase 4: Procurement Best Practices for Government Buyers


### Developing Effective RFPs for Charging Infrastructure


Procurement is where a municipality either preserves or forfeits its leverage for the next decade. The requirements that carry the most weight:


**Scope definition.** State clearly what is included: hardware, software, installation, commissioning, maintenance, driver support, and reporting. Ambiguity here produces change orders later.


**Performance requirements.** Specify uptime and session success separately, because they measure different things. Uptime measures whether a station is available. Session success measures whether drivers actually complete charges. A network can report strong uptime and still fail drivers routinely, which is why the second metric belongs in the contract.


[OCPP compliance](https://www.ampup.io/blog/what-is-ocpp-complete-standards-guide) **, specified by version.** The Open Charge Point Protocol is what allows a city to change software vendors without replacing hardware, or change hardware without replacing software. Specifying it by version is the single most effective anti-lock-in provision available to a municipal buyer, and it costs nothing at procurement.


**Buy America compliance** where federal funds are involved, including documentation requirements from the vendor.


**Prevailing wage and local hiring** consistent with your municipal code and any grant conditions.


**Payment and accessibility standards.** Contactless payment, a payment path that does not require an app or account, ADA-compliant station design and approach, and multilingual interface support.


**Data ownership.** State plainly that the city owns its utilization, session, and energy data in an exportable format, during and after the contract term. This is frequently overlooked and expensive to discover later.


### Single-Vendor vs. Multi-Vendor Strategies


**Single-vendor advantages.** Simplified operations, one support relationship, one invoice, and potential volume pricing. Attractive for smaller deployments and for cities with limited staff capacity.


**Multi-vendor advantages.** Preserved competition at each expansion phase, no exposure to a single manufacturer's product roadmap or financial health, and the ability to match hardware to site conditions.


**The practical resolution** is a hardware-agnostic software platform. When your management software supports multiple manufacturers, you get single-vendor operational simplicity with multi-vendor procurement flexibility. Your second phase can competitively bid hardware without a parallel software contract or a fragmented operations picture. AmpUp's[charging management platform](https://www.ampup.io/products/ev-charging-management-software) supports[130+ charger makes and models](https://www.ampup.io/resources/approved-ev-charger-manufacturers) for exactly this reason.


**Pilot before scale.** A first phase that deploys two manufacturers on a common platform gives you real operational data on reliability and service responsiveness before you commit to a network-wide standard.


**Regional standardization.** Coordinating hardware and software standards with neighboring jurisdictions improves pricing, simplifies the driver experience, and strengthens joint applications.


### Evaluation Criteria and Vendor Selection


- **Technical qualifications.** Relevant experience, certifications, and municipal references you can actually call. Ask references about year three, not installation.
- **Financial stability.** Years in operation, funding position, and municipal client base. Charging is a consolidating industry, and a vendor that does not survive your contract term is an expensive problem.
- **Proposed solution.**[Equipment specifications](https://www.ampup.io/blog/commercial-ev-charging-station-buyers-guide-2026) , software capabilities, integration options, and a maintenance plan with named response times.
- **Third-party validation.** Independent vetting, such as inclusion on the[EPRI Vetted Product List](https://www.ampup.io/blog/driving-forward-ampup-joins-the-epri-vetted-product-list) , gives you an outside check on vendor claims.
- **Total cost of ownership.** Evaluate on a ten-year basis including software fees, maintenance, payment processing, and expected replacement. Installed price alone reliably selects the wrong vendor.
- **Service response.** Local presence, dispatch time, and the share of faults resolved remotely. That last number drives your real maintenance cost more than any other factor.
- **Warranty and lifecycle.** Coverage terms and realistic equipment life, generally seven to ten years.


Ask each vendor what support looks like at 9 PM on a Saturday, because that is when a resident will be standing at a station that will not start. The answer separates proposals quickly. For a deeper look at platform evaluation criteria, see our guide to[choosing EV charging software](https://www.ampup.io/blog/ev-charging-software-platform-guide) .


### Contract Negotiation and Performance Standards


- **Service level agreements.** Uptime and session success standards, response time commitments by severity, and the measurement methodology. Specify who measures and how disputes are resolved.
- **Liquidated damages.** A financial consequence for sustained non-performance. Without one, your SLA is a statement of intent.
- **Change order process.** Defined scope adjustment procedure with pricing methodology agreed in advance.
- **Insurance requirements.** General liability, professional liability, and workers compensation consistent with your risk management standards.
- **Data ownership and reporting.** Format, frequency, and export rights, plus a clear statement that the data is the city's property.
- **Exit provisions.** Equipment ownership at termination, data transfer obligations, transition assistance, and a defined notice period. Negotiate these when the relationship is good.


## Phase 5: Installation, Permitting, and Project Management


### Navigating the Permitting Process


Municipal projects face the same permitting requirements as private ones, with the occasional advantage of internal coordination.


- **Building and electrical permits** , with inspections at rough-in and final
- **Right-of-way permits** for work in public streets and sidewalks, including traffic control plans
- **ADA compliance review** , covering accessible space dimensions, approach paths, and reach ranges at the charger
- **Environmental review.** CEQA in California, NEPA where federal funds are involved. Most charging projects qualify for categorical exemptions or exclusions, but confirm early rather than assuming.
- **Historic preservation review** for work in historic districts, which can affect equipment placement, screening, and finishes
- **Timeline.** Budget 3 to 6 months for permitting


Cities running charging programs are in an unusual position: they can streamline their own permitting. Several jurisdictions have adopted over-the-counter EV charger permitting with defined review timelines. Doing so accelerates your own projects and every private installation in your jurisdiction.


### Coordinating Utility Service Upgrades


- **Interconnection application** submitted as early as possible, since utility engineering review is frequently the longest single step
- **Service panel and transformer work** , including any required easements for utility equipment
- **Trenching and conduit** , which should be sized for planned future capacity rather than current need, since retrofitting costs substantially more
- **Make-ready program coordination** , which has its own timeline and inspection requirements layered onto the standard process
- **Expedited municipal processes** where your utility offers them, which is worth asking about directly


### Managing Installation and Construction


- **Site preparation.** Parking surface work, striping, wheel stops or bollards, and signage foundations
- **Electrical contractor coordination.** Scheduling around inspections and utility work, which rarely proceeds exactly as planned
- **ADA compliance verification.** Confirm accessible spaces, approach paths, and reach ranges against the approved drawings before final inspection, since correcting this after installation is expensive
- **Signage.** Wayfinding to the site, instructions at the station, pricing disclosure, and contact information for support
- **Testing and commissioning.** Verify every port initiates and completes a session, that payment processes correctly, and that the station reports properly to the management platform before public launch
- **Timeline.** Budget 6 to 12 months from contract execution to operational


Our[commercial EV charger installation guide](https://www.ampup.io/blog/electrician-guide-ev-charger-installation) walks through the electrical and construction sequence in more detail.


Do not skip commissioning. A port that was never verified end to end is a port that will fail on a resident in week one, and first impressions of a public network are difficult to reverse.


### NEVI Compliance Requirements


For NEVI-funded projects, federal minimum standards under 23 CFR 680 apply:


- **Minimum 150 kW** simultaneous charging capacity per port
- **Four ports minimum** per site, with connector requirements that now commonly include both CCS1 and NACS. The NACS requirement took effect in 2025, and most states now require dual-connector configurations. See our[NACS vs. CCS guide](https://www.ampup.io/blog/nacs-vs-ccs-future-proof-your-ev-charger-strategy) for specification detail.
- **Payment terminals** accepting multiple payment methods, including a path that does not require a membership or app
- **97% average annual uptime** per port, with automated quarterly reporting through the federal reporting system
- **ADA compliance** in station design and site approach
- **Buy America provisions** for equipment and components


Note the distinction between the federal 97% uptime floor and the operational standards worth holding yourself to. The federal requirement is a compliance minimum, not a performance target.


## Operations, Maintenance, and Ongoing Management


### Establishing Operations and Maintenance Plans


Charging infrastructure is a connected electrical asset, not a set-and-forget installation. A baseline plan:


- **Daily:** automated monitoring with alerting on faults, targeting 99.9% uptime. This requires[networked chargers](https://www.ampup.io/blog/networked-vs-non-networked-ev-chargers) , since non-networked equipment cannot report status remotely.
- **Quarterly:** visual inspection of cables, connectors, mounting hardware, signage, and payment terminals, plus a review of session logs for anomalies
- **Annually:** full system test, protective device verification, firmware and software review, enclosure seal inspection, and cable condition assessment
- **Reactive maintenance:** a defined response window, commonly 24 to 48 hours for a station-down condition, with escalation for high-traffic sites
- **Software updates and security patches** applied on a managed schedule rather than ad hoc
- **Cleaning and cosmetic upkeep.** A stained, tagged, or damaged station reads as neglect regardless of whether it works, and public perception of your network is built on that impression.
- **Weather response.** Snow removal that actually clears the charging spaces and the approach path, not just the drive aisle


### Managing User Experience and Customer Support


- **24/7 driver support.** A charging fault at 9 PM needs a resolution path that does not wait for business hours. Whether staffed internally or through your platform provider, the number on the station has to reach someone.
- [Mobile app](https://www.ampup.io/products/ev-charging-app-for-drivers) **.** Station location, real-time availability, pricing disclosure, and payment. Drivers check availability before they drive, and a station that does not appear in an app is functionally invisible.
- **On-station instructions.** Clear, brief, and multilingual where your community requires it.
- **Feedback and complaint resolution.** A documented path with defined response times. Complaints are also your earliest signal of an equipment problem.
- **Community engagement.** Monitor local social channels. Municipal charging complaints surface there well before they reach a service ticket.


### Setting Pricing and Access Policies


Pricing is policy, and it belongs in front of your council rather than buried in a vendor configuration.


**Free versus paid.** Free charging drives high early utilization, produces no cost recovery, and encourages vehicles to occupy ports after charging completes. Most cities move to paid charging within one to two years. Where free charging serves a specific policy goal, scope it to specific sites or specific users rather than the whole network.


**Pricing structure.** Energy-based pricing, commonly $0.30 to $0.50 per kWh, is more transparent to drivers than time-based pricing and is required or preferred in a growing number of states. Time-based pricing, commonly $1 to $2 per hour, remains in use where metering requirements make energy-based pricing impractical. Check your state's weights and measures requirements before selecting, since some states require certified metering such a s[CTEP certification](https://www.ampup.io/blog/ctep-certified-ev-chargers) in California.


**Discounted rates** for residents, income-qualified users, or[off-peak sessions](https://www.ampup.io/blog/time-of-use-ev-charging-rates) . Straightforward to implement when your platform supports user groups, and a practical way to serve access goals without making the whole network free.


**Idle fees** , commonly around $5 per hour after charging completes, to encourage turnover at high-demand sites. Disclose them clearly at the station and in the app.


**Fleet integration.** Municipal vehicles use the same infrastructure with separate accounting, so public and fleet costs are tracked distinctly.


**Special programs** for transit riders, municipal employees, or local business customers, where they support a defined policy objective.


If you are setting rates for the first time, AmpUp's[pricing recommendation engine](https://www.ampup.io/blog/ev-charging-pricing-recommendation-engine) models rates against local utilization and cost data.


#### Weights and Measures Requirements


Selling electricity by the kilowatt-hour makes a charging station a commercial measuring device, which brings it under state weights and measures law. This is a procurement question more than a pricing question, because the requirement attaches to the hardware.


What it means in practice:


- **Certified metering.** States that have adopted the NIST Handbook 44 provisions for electric vehicle fueling systems require chargers with type-certified meters. Selecting non-certified hardware eliminates per-kWh pricing as an option for the life of that equipment.
- **California requirements.** Chargers must meet[CTEP certification](https://www.ampup.io/blog/ctep-certified-ev-chargers) requirements, administered through the Division of Measurement Standards, with registration and periodic inspection handled by county sealers.
- **Registration and inspection.** Most states with requirements treat chargers like fuel dispensers: an initial device registration, periodic accuracy inspection, and a fee per device.
- **Procurement implication.** Put certification in the RFP. Confirming it during vendor evaluation costs nothing. Discovering it after installation means either replacing hardware or defaulting permanently to time-based pricing.


Check with your state weights and measures agency before finalizing hardware specifications, since adoption and enforcement timelines vary considerably by state.


### Achieving 98.5%+ Charging Session Success Rates


Public networks are judged by whether a charge starts. Session success rate, the share of initiated sessions that complete successfully, is the metric that reflects that experience, and it has historically been weak across the industry.


AmpUp's platform delivers a 98.5% charging session success rate. What produces that number:


- **Real-time monitoring with automated alerting** , so faults are identified before a resident reports them
- **Remote diagnostics and resolution.** AmpUp's[KlooBot AI diagnostics](https://www.ampup.io/blog/ampup-kloobot-ai-ev-charger-diagnostics) performs remote root-cause analysis on charger faults, resolving many issues without a site visit and identifying the correct fix when a visit is required.
- **Predictive maintenance** using performance data to catch degradation before failure
- **Driver support** that reduces user error and abandoned sessions, a meaningful share of apparent equipment failures
- [Hardware quality and regular verification](https://www.ampup.io/blog/ev-charger-reliability-testing) , including periodic end-to-end session testing
- **Backup capacity** at high-traffic locations, so a single fault does not take a site offline
- **Root cause tracking across sites** , which catches equipment patterns before they scale across the network


### **Data Collection and Public Transparency**


Publish your numbers. A public dashboard showing port count, utilization, uptime, and energy delivered does more for program durability than any communications campaign, and it builds the record you need when you return for expansion funding.


What to track:


- **Utilization:** sessions per port, kWh delivered, session duration, and time-of-day patterns
- **Distribution:** usage by site and neighborhood, which tells you whether your access goals are being met in practice
- **Environmental impact:** emissions avoided and gasoline displaced, calculated with a documented methodology such as the[EPA greenhouse gas equivalencies calculator](https://www.epa.gov/energy/greenhouse-gases-equivalencies-calculator-calculations-and-references)
- **Financial performance:** operating costs, revenue, and net subsidy per port
- **Reliability:** uptime and session success by site


Report annually to council against the Phase 1 targets. Cities that report consistently get their expansion requests approved. Cities that go quiet after the ribbon-cutting get audited.


Consider open data publication for researchers and regional planners. It costs little and builds credibility with the regional bodies whose funding decisions affect you.


## Equity and Environmental Justice Considerations


### Understanding the Justice40 Initiative and What Replaced It


If your planning documents reference Justice40, they need updating.


The Justice40 Initiative required that 40% of the overall benefits of covered federal investments flow to disadvantaged communities. It was established by executive order in January 2021 and rescinded in January 2025, along with the Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool that defined which communities qualified. The screening tool is no longer maintained on federal sites.


For municipal planners, the practical consequences:


- **Federal grant applications no longer carry Justice40 documentation requirements.** Applications drafted against the old framework need revision.
- **State requirements continue.** Many state energy office programs maintain their own equity criteria and screening tools, and these are now the operative federal-adjacent requirement.
- **Local policy is unaffected.** Equity commitments adopted by your council in a climate action plan or general plan remain fully binding municipal policy.


The planning implication is to ground your framework in criteria you control. A distribution approach built on your own housing and parking data, adopted through your own public process, does not change when federal policy does.


### Addressing Transportation Equity Gaps


The access gaps that municipal charging can actually address:


- **Renters and multifamily residents** without dedicated parking or the ability to install a circuit. This is the largest and most addressable gap, and it is the core case for public charging.
- **Lower-income households** for whom the used EV market is the realistic entry point. Charging access determines whether a used EV is practical.
- **Communities along high-traffic corridors** that bear disproportionate air quality burden, where transportation emissions reductions have the most direct local health effect.
- **Rural and unincorporated areas** with limited charging and longer distances between options, which are frequently overlooked in city-centered planning.
- **Residents who need language access** or who cannot use app-based payment, which is a design question as much as a site selection question.


### Designing Inclusive Programs and Pricing


Site selection alone does not produce access. Design decisions determine whether a station serves the people near it.


- **Income-qualified or resident discounts** , implemented through user groups in your charging platform
- **Multilingual support** across signage, app interface, and phone support, matched to the languages actually spoken in your community
- **Payment options that do not require an app or account.** Contactless card acceptance at the station is the practical baseline. Prepaid card compatibility extends access further.
- **Community-based organizations as partners** in outreach and site selection. They reach residents that municipal channels do not, and their endorsement carries weight yours may not.
- **Local hiring and workforce development** provisions in installation and maintenance contracts, which turn infrastructure spending into local employment


### Measuring and Reporting Equity Outcomes


- **Baseline data** on charging access and EV adoption by neighborhood, captured before deployment so you can show change
- **Usage patterns by site** , which is the practical proxy for who is being served, without collecting demographic data that raises privacy concerns
- **Community satisfaction** through periodic surveys and ongoing feedback channels
- **Economic impact** , including local hiring and contracting
- **Air quality trends** where local monitoring data supports the analysis


Report these alongside financial and reliability metrics rather than in a separate document. Integrated reporting keeps access goals in the same conversation as everything else the program is accountable for.


## Integration with Municipal Fleet Electrification


### Coordinating Public and Fleet Charging Infrastructure


Shared infrastructure is one of the strongest cost levers available to a city. Fire stations, public works yards, city hall, and library lots can serve[municipal fleet charging solutions](https://www.ampup.io/use-cases/ev-charging-management-for-fleets) during business hours and public charging on evenings and weekends.


Making it work requires:


- **Access rules by user group and time of day** , enforced by the EV charging platform rather than by signage
- **Cost allocation** between fleet and public usage, with usage tracking that supports internal chargeback
- **Electrical sizing for combined peak demand** , not fleet peak alone, since retrofitting capacity later costs multiples of building it in
- **Unified management** across both use cases, so your staff monitors one system rather than two


Our[fleet charging management guide](https://www.ampup.io/blog/fleet-charging-management-best-practices-a-complete-guide-for-fleet-operators) covers depot operations, load management, and driver protocols in depth.


### Leveraging Fleet Charging for Public Benefit


- **Operational credibility.** A city that has run electric vehicles through two winters can answer resident questions from experience rather than from a vendor brochure.
- **Visibility.** Municipal EVs charging at public sites normalize the technology and demonstrate the city's commitment more effectively than a press release.
- **Maintenance capacity.** Fleet maintenance staff familiar with charging equipment become a resource for the public network.
- **Procurement leverage.** Combining fleet and public charging volume improves pricing and reduces administrative overhead across both.
- **Data.** Fleet charging patterns inform public network planning, particularly around load management and equipment selection.


### Depot Charging at Municipal Facilities


- **Police and fire stations.** Emergency vehicle charging with backup power provisions, since these facilities cannot lose charging capability during an outage.
- **Public works yards.** Heavy-duty vehicle charging with higher power requirements and different dwell patterns than light-duty fleet.
- **Transit facilities.** Bus depot charging at a scale that requires direct utility coordination and typically dedicated infrastructure.
- **Parking structures.** Combined employee and public charging, with ventilation and fire code considerations specific to enclosed structures.
- **Load management across all of it.** Municipal facilities frequently share electrical service with other city operations, which makes coordinated load management a requirement rather than an optimization.


## Regional Coordination and Partnerships


### Working with Your Metropolitan Planning Organization


Your MPO decides which transportation projects receive federal funding in your metro area. For EV charging, it matters for three reasons: money, timing, and data. Cities that engage their MPO early tend to do better on all three.


- **Get into the TIP early.** Projects using federal transportation funds generally must appear in the MPO’s Transportation Improvement Program before funds can be committed. TIP updates run on fixed cycles, often annual, so a project that misses a window can wait a year. Contact your MPO during the needs assessment, not after you have a site list.
- **Know which funds the MPO controls.** CMAQ is the best known, but in larger metro areas the MPO also selects projects for its share of Surface Transportation Block Grant (STBG) funds. Both can support charging infrastructure.
- **Use the MPO’s data and plans.** Many MPOs have published regional EV readiness plans, adoption forecasts, and travel demand models. These can anchor your needs assessment and strengthen grant applications, particularly for smaller cities without in-house modeling capacity.
- **Let the MPO lead regional efforts.** MPOs are eligible applicants for federal Charging and Fueling Infrastructure (CFI) grants and are well positioned to lead multi-jurisdiction applications, regional site prioritization, and shared procurements.
- **Ask for a seat at the table.** Many MPOs run EV or clean transportation working groups. Participation gives you early visibility into funding rounds and regional priorities.


### Collaborating with Neighboring Jurisdictions


- **Shared procurement.** Joint solicitations improve pricing and spread the administrative burden of a complex procurement across multiple staffs.
- **Standardized user experience.** Consistent branding, pricing structure, and payment methods across a metro area reduce driver confusion substantially.
- **Roaming agreements.** One account working across multiple jurisdictions is a meaningful convenience and requires platform interoperability rather than identical hardware.
- **Joint grant applications.** Multi-jurisdiction applications compete better for corridor funding than single-city requests, and they demonstrate the regional coordination that reviewers look for.


### **State and Federal Agency Engagement**


- **State energy office.** Grant administration, technical assistance, and current program status. Your most important external relationship in 2026.
- **State DOT.** Corridor planning, NEVI administration, and right-of-way coordination.
- **EPA regional offices.** Air quality program support and relevant grant programs.
- **National laboratories.** Modeling tools, technical analysis, and peer research, frequently available at no cost.
- **Clean Cities coalitions.** Regional coordinators with practical deployment experience and peer networks. An underused resource for cities early in the process.


### Private Sector and Utility Partnerships


- **Major employers.** Workplace charging reduces daytime public demand and extends the effective network without municipal capital.
- **Retail and hospitality.** Destination charging partnerships that serve visitors and support downtown businesses.
- **Property owner coalitions.** Multifamily property owners face a genuine cost barrier. A city that convenes them and connects them to utility programs can unlock charging it would never fund directly.
- **Utility advisory boards.** Participation gives you visibility into program design before it is finalized.
- **Auto dealerships.** Local adoption data and customer education partnerships.


### Community and Nonprofit Engagement


- **Environmental and community advocacy organizations** , which bring both scrutiny and, when engaged genuinely, support
- **Homeowner and tenant associations** , particularly for neighborhood-level site selection
- **Business improvement districts and downtown associations** , frequently willing to co-fund downtown charging
- **Public health organizations** , which can articulate the air quality case more credibly than city staff
- **Educational institutions** , for research partnerships, workforce development, and campus charging coordination


## Performance Monitoring and Network Optimization


### Key Performance Indicators for Municipal Networks


KPI Target


Charging session success rate 98.5%+


Infrastructure uptime 99.9%


Utilization (Level 2) 3 to 6 sessions per port per day


Geographic coverage Share of residents within a 5 to 10 minute drive


Cost recovery Percentage of operating costs covered by revenue


Subsidy per port Tracked annually by site type


Environmental impact Annual emissions avoided and gasoline displaced


User satisfaction Survey scores and complaint rate


Report utilization with a realistic ramp expectation. A new site reaching target utilization in month three is unusual, and a council that was told to expect it will read normal performance as failure.


### Data-Driven Expansion Planning


After six to twelve months of operation, patterns emerge that support genuine optimization:


- **High-demand sites** where queuing or session timeouts indicate capacity constraints. These are your clearest expansion candidates.
- **Underutilized sites.** Determine whether the issue is awareness, wayfinding, pricing, or location before deciding to relocate equipment.
- **Seasonal and event patterns.** Tourism, school calendars, and event venues produce predictable swings that should inform both expansion and pricing.
- **Session timeout and waitlist data** , which is a better capacity signal than raw utilization percentage.
- **Neighborhood-level usage** , which tells you whether distribution goals are being met in practice rather than in site selection.
- **Peer city comparison.** Benchmarking against cities of similar size and density provides context your own data cannot.


### Annual Reporting and Stakeholder Communication


- **City council presentations.** Progress against adopted targets, financial performance including subsidy, reliability, and distribution. Consistency of format year over year matters more than polish.
- **Public annual reports** in plain language and accessible formats.
- **Grant compliance reporting** to state and federal agencies on their required cadence.
- **Media and milestone communication.** Port count milestones, new site openings, and reliability performance.
- **Community meetings.** Continued engagement in neighborhoods where you have deployed and where you plan to.


### Long-Term Network Evolution


- **Technology refresh.** Plan for equipment replacement at seven to ten years, and budget for it from year one rather than treating it as a future problem.
- **Scaling for adoption growth.** Design electrical infrastructure and conduit for substantially more capacity than initial port count requires.
- **Emerging technology.** Megawatt charging, bidirectional charging, and wireless charging will affect specifications over the coming decade. Avoid committing to any of them prematurely while keeping infrastructure flexible.
- **Autonomous vehicle infrastructure.** Still speculative for most cities, but worth monitoring where automated fleet operations are being piloted locally.
- **Climate resilience.** Flooding, extreme heat, and wildfire risk all affect charging infrastructure site selection and design decisions, particularly for equipment expected to last a decade or more.


## Common Challenges and How Municipalities Overcome Them


### Limited Capital Budget and Competing Priorities


Charging competes with street maintenance, public safety, and every other capital need. Practical responses:


- Pursue utility make-ready programs aggressively, since they are the largest available offset and do not require a capital appropriation
- Phase deployment against confirmed funding rather than committing to a network size you cannot finance
- Pair public charging with fleet electrification funding where infrastructure is shared, which draws on a different budget line
- Use public-private partnership structures that shift capital burden for commercially viable sites, reserving municipal capital for sites the market will not serve


### Utility Capacity Constraints and Long Lead Times


- Engage your utility 18 to 24 months ahead of target energization
- Use load management to maximize deployment on existing electrical capacity
- Sequence your first phase toward sites with adequate existing service, so you have operational chargers while longer projects proceed
- Participate in make-ready programs, which fund the upgrade and often accelerate the utility's own scheduling


### Procurement Complexity and Grant Compliance


- Bring procurement and legal into Phase 1, not Phase 4. Their constraints shape what is possible.
- Request model RFP language from peer cities of similar size. Most will share it.
- Consider grant writing support for complex federal applications, particularly first-time applicants
- Use regional purchasing cooperatives, which reduce both cost and administrative burden


### Resistance from Stakeholders or Community Members


- Engage early and genuinely, before decisions are made rather than after
- Address concerns with data and peer city examples rather than advocacy
- Use a pilot to demonstrate viability before requesting a larger commitment
- Ensure outreach reaches beyond the residents who already attend city meetings


Common objections worth preparing for: subsidizing an affluent minority, parking space loss, equipment reliability, and cost. Each has a factual answer. Prepare them before the meeting rather than during it.


### Uncertainty About Long-Term Financial Sustainability


- Use conservative utilization assumptions and run sensitivity analysis on the downside case
- Consider[managed services contracts](https://www.ampup.io/products/ev-charger-operations-and-maintenance-service) that transfer operational risk and convert variable cost to predictable cost
- Use hybrid models in which cost recovery at high-traffic sites offsets access-driven locations
- Build in regular rate review, so pricing can adjust as utilization and costs change without requiring a new policy process each time


## Case Studies and Municipal Success Stories


The following are composite profiles drawn from common municipal deployment patterns rather than specific named jurisdictions. They illustrate approaches that recur across successful programs. For a documented public sector example, Connecticut regulators selected AmpUp's Adapt & Earn managed charging program to[scale statewide](https://www.ampup.io/blog/connecticut-scales-public-managed-ev-charging) , the only Cycle 1 pilot chosen for expansion.


### Small City Profile: Population Under 50,000


**Challenge.** Limited capital and a public works department with no staff capacity for a new program.


**Approach.** A ten-port Level 2 pilot at city hall and the public library, chosen for existing electrical capacity and municipal property control.


**Funding.** Utility make-ready program combined with a state energy office grant, covering the substantial majority of project cost.


**Outcome.** Steady utilization growth over the first year, expansion approved to roughly triple the initial port count.


**Lesson.** Start small, prove the concept, and build political support with operating data. A modest pilot that performs is a stronger case for expansion than an ambitious plan that has not been tested.


### Mid-Sized City Profile: Access-Focused Deployment


**Challenge.** Ensuring charging reaches neighborhoods with the lowest home charging access, where utilization forecasts are weakest and the commercial case does not stand alone.


**Approach.** Majority of ports sited in neighborhoods with high renter share and low off-street parking availability, with introductory free charging in year one.


**Partnership.** Community-based organizations engaged for outreach and site selection input rather than notification.


**Outcome.** Substantial usage from target neighborhoods and strong community satisfaction, with the subsidy requirement identified and budgeted upfront rather than discovered.


**Lesson.** Authentic community engagement produces better site selection decisions, and naming the subsidy as a deliberate public service decision is a stronger political position than hoping the economics work out.


### Large City Profile: Regional Corridor Charging


**Challenge.** Highway corridor gaps limiting regional travel, beyond the capacity of any single jurisdiction to address.


**Approach.** Multi-jurisdiction corridor application coordinated across adjacent cities, the county, and the state DOT.


**Partnership.** Private land owners for site access, state DOT for corridor planning, neighboring jurisdictions for joint application.


**Outcome.** Federal corridor funding was secured, with sites phased over roughly two years.


**Lesson.** Regional coordination multiplies both impact and funding leverage. Corridor funding is structurally designed for multi-jurisdiction applications, and single-city requests compete poorly.


### Innovative Model Profile: Fleet and Public Shared Infrastructure


**Challenge.** Municipal fleet charging needs competing with public access goals for the same limited capital.


**Approach.** Dual-access sites at fire stations, libraries, and public works yards, with electrical infrastructure sized for combined demand.


**Technology.** Platform-enforced access rules prioritizing fleet vehicles during business hours and opening ports to public use on evenings and weekends.


**Outcome.** Meaningful capital savings through shared infrastructure, with high combined utilization across both use cases.


**Lesson.** Flexible access policy maximizes return on infrastructure investment. The constraint is platform capability, not electrical capacity.


## Looking Ahead: Emerging Trends and Future Considerations


### NACS Transition


The North American Charging Standard has become the dominant connector across the light-duty market, and the transition is largely complete on new deployments. Federal NEVI requirements have incorporated NACS since 2025, and most states now require dual-connector configurations covering both CCS1 and NACS.


For municipal planners the practical questions are retrofit and specification. Existing CCS-only DC fast sites may warrant retrofit depending on local vehicle mix. New DC fast procurement should specify dual connectors. Level 2 is largely unaffected, since the J1772 connector and adapters cover the installed base.


### Megawatt Charging for Heavy-Duty Vehicles


The Megawatt Charging System standard targets vehicles that cannot be served by existing DC fast charging: long-haul trucks, transit buses, and heavy municipal equipment. Infrastructure requirements are substantial, frequently including dedicated utility infrastructure.


Relevant to cities with transit operations, port activity, or freight corridors. For most municipalities this is a monitoring item rather than a planning item, but cities with transit depots should be in conversation with their utility now, because the lead times are long.


### Vehicle-to-Grid and Bidirectional Charging


Bidirectional charging lets vehicles return energy to a building or the grid. Municipal applications include using fleet vehicles as backup power for critical facilities and participating in utility grid services programs for revenue.


The technology is real but deployment remains limited, and the regulatory and utility interconnection frameworks are still developing in most jurisdictions. The practical step today is specifying ISO 15118 communication capability in new procurement, which preserves the option without requiring a commitment.


### Autonomous Vehicles and Automated Charging


Automated charging, including robotic connection and wireless charging, is under development primarily for fleet and autonomous applications. Accessibility is a genuine secondary benefit, since automated connection addresses a real barrier for drivers with limited mobility.


Not a near-term planning consideration for most municipalities, though cities hosting autonomous vehicle pilots should track how charging infrastructure requirements develop.


### Climate Resilience and Adaptation Planning


Charging infrastructure installed today will operate for a decade or more under conditions that are changing.


- **Extreme heat** reduces charging performance and shortens equipment life. Shade structures and equipment rated for higher ambient temperatures are worth the cost in hot climates.
- **Flooding.** Elevate equipment above projected flood levels and avoid site selection critical infrastructure in flood-prone locations, particularly at emergency response facilities.
- **Wildfire and outage risk.** Backup power at critical facilities, and consideration of undergrounding where feasible.
- **Long-horizon planning.** The electrical infrastructure supporting charging, including conduit and service capacity, has a far longer life than the chargers themselves. Size and site plan it accordingly.

## Municipal EV Charging FAQs


**How much does a municipal EV charging network cost?** Budget roughly $3,000 to $7,000 per installed Level 2 port and $75,000 to $150,000 per DC fast port, plus electrical service upgrades ranging from $20,000 to $150,000 per site depending on distance to adequate service. Operating costs including electricity, maintenance, software, payment processing, and support are ongoing and should be budgeted separately from capital. Break-even typically falls between three and seven years depending on utilization.


**Is NEVI funding still available to municipalities in 2026?** Yes. NEVI was paused in February 2025 and restored following litigation and revised FHWA guidance issued in August 2025. States have been reopening solicitations, and the revised guidance allows states that certify their corridors as fully built out to direct remaining funds to off-corridor community charging locations. Federal cost share remains up to 80%. Round timing and availability vary significantly by state, so start with your state energy office or DOT.


**Does the Justice40 requirement still apply to EV charging grants?** No. The Justice40 Initiative and the federal Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool were rescinded in January 2025, and federal applications no longer carry Justice40 documentation requirements. State equity criteria and local policy commitments remain in effect, and many state energy office programs maintain their own screening tools and distribution requirements. Cities with equity goals adopted by council should ground their framework in local data and state tools rather than the rescinded federal framework.


**What uptime should a city require in an EV charging RFP?** Require both an uptime standard and a session success standard, since they measure different things. NEVI-funded projects must meet 97% average annual uptime per port under federal minimum standards. Session success rate, the share of initiated sessions that complete, is the metric that reflects actual driver experience. AmpUp delivers a 98.5% session success rate and 99.9% uptime.


**How long does a municipal EV charging project take?** Plan for 18 to 36 months from initial assessment to operational chargers. Needs assessment typically takes two to four months, site selection three to six months, funding four to eight months, procurement and installation six to twelve months, and permitting three to six months running partially in parallel. Utility service upgrades are the most common cause of delay, ranging from six to eighteen months depending on scope.


**What role does a metropolitan planning organization (MPO) play in municipal EV charging?** An MPO programs federal transportation funds for its region, including CMAQ and a share of STBG, and those projects generally must appear in its Transportation Improvement Program. MPOs also maintain regional EV plans and travel data and can lead multi-city grant applications. Engage your MPO during the needs assessment so your projects line up with the next TIP cycle.


**Should a city charge for public EV charging or offer it free?** Most cities move to paid charging within one to two years of launch. Free charging drives high early utilization but produces no cost recovery and encourages vehicles to occupy ports after charging completes. A common approach is modest energy-based pricing with idle fees, plus discounted rates for residents or income-qualified users at specific sites. Where free charging serves a defined policy goal, scope it to specific sites rather than the whole network.


**How do cities avoid vendor lock-in with charging infrastructure?** Specify OCPP compliance by version in the RFP, select a hardware-agnostic management platform that supports multiple manufacturers, retain ownership of charging data in exportable form, and define equipment ownership and transition obligations at contract end. These provisions cost nothing at procurement and preserve competitive leverage for the life of the network.


**Can municipal fleet and public charging share the same infrastructure?** Yes, and it is one of the strongest cost levers available. Sites at fire stations, public works yards, city hall, and libraries can serve fleet vehicles during business hours and the public on evenings and weekends. Success requires a platform that enforces access rules by user group and time of day, allocates energy costs between fleet and public usage, and manages load across combined demand. Size the electrical service for the combined peak.
